title: What is @SecondaryTable, how does it let one entity span multiple tables, and when should you use it?
keyPoints: @SecondaryTable maps one JPA entity across two or more physical tables that share the same primary key.
Fields are routed to the secondary table with @Column(table="secondary_table_name"); fields without a table attribute default to the primary table.
Hibernate transparently joins the tables on read and splits writes across them on save.
Use it for legacy schemas, separating hot/cold columns, or isolating sensitive data (KYC documents) into a separate table.
The secondary table is joined eagerly by default; for genuinely cold data, a lazy @OneToOne may be more efficient.
@SecondaryTable is a mapping convenience, not a sharding or scaling tool: both tables live in the same database.

s1_definition.oneliner: @SecondaryTable maps one entity across multiple tables sharing the primary key; route fields with @Column(table="...") and Hibernate joins on read and splits on write automatically.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **@SecondaryTable** – declares an additional table that shares the primary key with the main @Table, allowing one entity to span multiple physical tables.
- **@PrimaryKeyJoinColumn** – specifies the column in the secondary table that joins back to the primary table's PK.
- **@Column(table="...")** – routes a field to the secondary table; fields without this attribute default to the primary table.
- **Transparent join** – Hibernate generates a JOIN on read and splits INSERTs/UPDATEs across both tables on write.
- **Use cases** – legacy schemas with split records, separating hot (frequently-read) from cold (rarely-read) columns, and isolating sensitive data.
s1_definition.analogy: A customer's full record at National Bank of India is one logical thing, but the data lives in two filing cabinets: the everyday cabinet holds name and balance, while a separate secure cabinet holds the KYC documents and address proof. @SecondaryTable is the clerk who knows both cabinets belong to the same customer number, fetches from both when you ask for the customer, and files into both when you update, so you deal with one customer, not two cabinets.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  @SecondaryTable Mapping
  ============================================

  Primary Table: accounts        Secondary Table: account_kyc
  +------------------+           +-----------------------+
  | account_id (PK)  |<--------->| account_id (PK + FK)  |
  | holder_name      |           | pan                   |
  | balance          |           | aadhaar_doc           |
  +------------------+           +-----------------------+

  One Entity: Account
  ============================================
  @Table(name = "accounts")
  @SecondaryTable(name = "account_kyc")

  Fields without table attr   -> accounts (primary)
  @Column(table="account_kyc") -> account_kyc (secondary)

  Read:  SELECT a.*, k.pan, k.aadhaar_doc
         FROM accounts a JOIN account_kyc k
         ON a.account_id = k.account_id

  Write: INSERT INTO accounts (...)
         INSERT INTO account_kyc (...)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
@SecondaryTable lets a single JPA entity map its fields across two or more physical tables that share the same primary key. Rajesh declares the main table with @Table and each extra table with @SecondaryTable, telling Hibernate the join column with @PrimaryKeyJoinColumn. Then he routes individual fields to the secondary table with @Column(table="..."), while fields without that attribute default to the primary table. On a read, Hibernate generates a join on the shared key and assembles one entity, and on a save it splits the inserts or updates across both tables.

At National Bank of India, the accounts table holds the everyday columns (name, balance) and a secondary account_kyc table holds the PAN and document blobs, yet the code deals with one Account entity. Pankaj reaches for this in legacy schemas where records were split, for separating hot from cold columns, and for isolating sensitive KYC data into a table with stricter access controls.

The senior cautions are that the secondary table is joined eagerly by default, so if the secondary columns are genuinely cold a lazy @OneToOne may be more efficient. He also ensures secondary columns are nullable so the entity loads even without a secondary row, and he remembers that @SecondaryTable is a mapping convenience, not a sharding tool, because both tables live in the same database.

Remember one sentence: @SecondaryTable maps one entity across multiple tables sharing the primary key, with fields routed via @Column(table="...") and Hibernate transparently joining on read and splitting on write.
